proof_review: The theorem uses actual transitive string actions and maximal-omission intransitivity. Each label has an eligible edge, since otherwise adjoining that mark would leave the omission intransitive. The acquired paired-cut bound 2r<=n therefore ensures a label with exactly one eligible edge. Such an edge is a bridge of the full coloured permutation graph: all other edges of that colour remain inside omission orbits and all other labels preserve those orbits.

The separated-cut lemma applies the outside-side bound to actual A and, in reversed order, actual D. The reversed indices are r-1-j and r-1-g, yielding |D|>=2r-j-g-1. Deleting the two bridges gives connected middle region M. A path from its first endpoint b to its second endpoint c must contain each i<k<j: if k were absent, commute its higher-index letters to the beginning, where each fixes b by the unique i-crossing; all remaining letters commute with rho_j, which fixes b since j>=i+2. This contradicts rho_j moving c. This explicit argument works even if the path contains internal i-edges; alternatively choose the path in the connected i-omission graph on B, avoiding all i-edges, and bridge simplicity keeps it inside M. Thus |M|>=j-i and n>=2r+h-g, without a local eligibility substitution.

Assuming no perfect cut, reverse once to obtain a cut with a shared mark on the right, then choose maximal such cut index i in that fixed orientation. The primitive interval supplied by the acquired orbit-budget theorem must be on the right because each shared mark acts on it. Thus L fixes B, and the head theorem applies. Interior singleton and endpoint singleton cases are explicitly removed by their correct different arguments. If i=0, renaming the sides to follow the final tail is legitimate because L is empty.

If every mark after the largest shared h were paired, the whole tail is intransitive on the ambient set because it fixes nonempty A. The exact ambient-interval theorem applies even if the tail is transitive on its own support: its actual nontrivial orbit is still a proper ambient orbit. It gives a bound at least as strong as the weak one used. Combining with the head budget forces 2r<=n+1, so a later unique cut j exists. Choosing the least one proves all intervening colours have two ambient eligible edges.

The j-edge lies in B since its mark belongs to the tail supported there. Deleting the i and j bridges gives A,M,D in series and the j-orbits C=A union M,D. Maximality of i excludes shared marks to the right of j. A shared mark to its left exists because the cut is assumed nonperfect. The least such mark g is therefore well defined, and j>=i+2.

For j<r-1, the primitive interval must lie left of j. If the primitive side were D, G_>j would fix D and the reversed last-mark lemma with positive crossing r-1-j would apply with first side C. The original rho0 acts on C: for i>0 its nonempty support is inside A; for i=0 it contains the original i-bridge, now internal to C. This would give n>=2r. Hence the primitive side is C, G_>j fixes C and the reversed tail support is in C. For j=r-1 the right subgroup is empty; reversed endpoint last-mark exclusion gives g>0, and the tail containing rho0 must act on C. These endpoint cases need no new equality classification.

The reversed head budget is 2(r-1-g)<=n-|Y|-1, with Y=supp(G_<g). The separated-region lemma uses h active on A and g active on D, so g<=h would give n>=2r+h-g>=2r, impossible. Thus g>h. The two tails contain every original mark; no point is fixed by all marks in this nontrivial transitive action, hence X union Y is the whole point set.

Every mark in the middle interval h<l<g is ambient-paired by the minimal choice of j. Its actual subgroup fixes the i-omission sides setwise, so is ambient-intransitive, and its support lies in X intersection Y. The acquired interval bound gives 2(g-h-1)<=|X intersection Y|; for the empty interval the same weak bound is immediate. Summing with the two outside budgets gives exactly 2r<=n+2, contrary to the stated strict range. The correct reversed index and the +4 in the final identity are both checked.

The theorem proves a perfect split, whose crossing involution may retain internal edges. It does not assert that this crossing is a pure transposition, that the wider 2r>n+1 boundary is settled, or that the stability bijection and enumerative constants follow without their remaining proofs. The small-degree action qualification of the initial fracture theorem remains an explicit separate principal-assembly obligation.
